# Final Report: High-Dosage Math Tutoring in Urban Middle Schools

**Spencer Foundation research grant (fictional award PB-SP-MTE-2020-01)**
Principal Investigator: Rachel M. Ostrander, Velmarden University
Co-Principal Investigator: Marcus J. Treviño, Velmarden University
Project period: 1 August 2020 – 31 July 2024
Total award: $748,000

Report submitted: October 2024

---

## 1. Overview

This project evaluated the impact of a high-dosage mathematics tutoring programme on the achievement, attitudes and course-taking trajectories of students in grades 6–8 in the Cedarquill Metropolitan School District (CQMSD), a large urban district serving a predominantly low-income, racially diverse student population. The study combined a cluster-randomised controlled trial (RCT) with a qualitative investigation of tutor practices and experiences.

The project was funded entirely by the Spencer Foundation. The $748,000 grant supported the research and evaluation activities: research staff salaries, data collection, instrument development, qualitative fieldwork, and dissemination. The actual RatioWeave-Tutor tutoring programme—tutor salaries and benefits, training, materials, and supervision—was funded by CQMSD using a combination of district operating funds and federal Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) allocations. The project was not funded by the National Science Foundation and does not constitute NSF-supported research.

## 2. Programme Description

The tutoring model, called RatioWeave-Tutor, provided three 45-minute sessions per week of small-group tutoring (3 students per tutor) during the regular school day, replacing a non-academic elective period. Tutors were full-time, salaried paraprofessionals with at least a bachelor's degree, who received 80 hours of initial training and weekly coaching from a district mathematics coach. The curriculum was aligned to the district's adopted middle-grades mathematics sequence and emphasised conceptual understanding, procedural fluency and problem-solving.

## 3. Research Design

### 3.1 Randomised Controlled Trial

- **Unit of randomisation:** School (to avoid within-school contamination).
- **Sample:** 42 schools were eligible; 38 agreed to participate. Schools were stratified by baseline proficiency rate (above/below district median) and percentage of students receiving free or reduced-price lunch (above/below 80%), then randomly assigned within strata: 19 treatment, 19 control.
- **Student sample:** 4,217 students in the analytic sample (2,118 treatment; 2,099 control) after attrition. The original enrolled sample was 4,530 students; attrition was 6.9%.
- **Demographics of analytic sample:** 47% Black, 31% Hispanic, 12% White, 10% other; 83% eligible for free or reduced-price lunch; 14% receiving special education services; 19% classified as English learners.
- **Outcome measures:** (a) State mathematics assessment scaled scores (primary outcome, administered spring of each year); (b) Researcher-developed assessment of algebraic reasoning (secondary outcome, pre/post each year); (c) Mathematics self-efficacy scale (Likert, 12 items, α = 0.88).
- **Analytic approach:** Intent-to-treat (ITT) estimates from two-level hierarchical linear models (students nested in schools), with randomisation-stratum fixed effects and baseline covariates (prior-year math score, gender, race/ethnicity, FRL status, EL status, special education status). Effect sizes reported as Hedges' g.

### 3.2 Qualitative Component

Semi-structured interviews with 48 tutors (25 in Year 2, 23 in Year 3), purposively sampled across schools and experience levels. Interviews lasted 45–75 minutes and were audio-recorded and transcribed. Analysis used a priori and emergent codes in NVivo, with inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ) of 0.81 across two coders (Treviño and a trained doctoral student).

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Impact on Mathematics Achievement

After two years of treatment (the primary pre-registered endpoint):

- **State math assessment:** Treatment students scored higher by **0.21 SD** (Hedges' g = 0.21, 95% CI [0.09, 0.33], p = 0.001). The effect was statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
- **Algebraic reasoning assessment:** Treatment effect of **0.28 SD** (95% CI [0.14, 0.42], p < 0.001).
- **Mathematics self-efficacy:** Treatment effect of **0.13 SD** (95% CI [0.01, 0.25], p = 0.04).

Subgroup analyses (pre-registered):

- Students in the bottom quartile of baseline math scores: effect on state assessment of **0.34 SD** (95% CI [0.16, 0.52]).
- Hispanic students: **0.26 SD** (95% CI [0.10, 0.42]).
- Black students: **0.19 SD** (95% CI [0.05, 0.33]).
- English learners: **0.24 SD** (95% CI [0.06, 0.42]).

### 4.2 Attendance and Dosage

Among treatment students, the median tutoring attendance rate was **87%** of scheduled sessions over two years. In an exploratory comparison of the 1,614 treatment students attending at least 80% of sessions with the control sample, the adjusted difference was **0.27 SD** (95% CI [0.13, 0.41]). Attendance was not randomised; this selected-sample association does not identify a causal effect of higher attendance or establish an effect larger than the ITT estimate.

### 4.3 Cost

The per-student cost of the RatioWeave-Tutor programme was **$3,400 per year**, including tutor salaries and benefits, training, materials and supervision. This cost was borne by CQMSD; the Spencer Foundation grant covered only the research and evaluation. The per-student cost figure does not include the opportunity cost of the replaced elective period.

### 4.4 Qualitative Findings

Four themes emerged from tutor interviews:

1. **Responsive pacing.** Tutors described adjusting lesson pace based on real-time observation of student work, but reported difficulty diagnosing specific misconceptions quickly, especially in rational number operations and proportional reasoning.
2. **Relationship building.** Tutors emphasised that consistent, small-group interaction built trust, which they saw as essential for students to reveal confusion.
3. **Curriculum rigidity.** 31 of 48 tutors (65%) felt the scripted curriculum limited their ability to pursue productive student thinking.
4. **Isolation.** Tutors had limited interaction with classroom teachers; 38 of 48 (79%) reported meeting with the student's regular math teacher fewer than twice per semester.

## 5. Limitations

1. The study was conducted in a single urban district; generalisability to suburban or rural settings is unknown.
2. The control condition was business-as-usual instruction; we cannot isolate which components of the tutoring model (small group size, dosage, curriculum alignment, tutor training) drove the effects.
3. We measured outcomes only through the end of the two-year treatment period; longer-term persistence of effects is unknown.
4. The qualitative sample of 48 tutors, while purposive, may not capture the full range of tutor experiences.
5. The study did not incorporate any technology-based or AI-assisted tutoring tools; all instruction was delivered face-to-face by human tutors without adaptive software.

## 6. Data and Materials

De-identified student-level data (achievement scores, demographics, attendance) are deposited in the Velmarden Center for Education Research restricted archive, record PB-MTE-DATA-01, under a restricted-use agreement. Interview transcripts are available upon request with IRB approval. The RatioWeave-Tutor curriculum materials are proprietary to CQMSD and are not publicly available.

## 7. Publications from This Grant

See separate publications list for the five publications resulting from this project.

# Team and Institutional Resources

*As of September 2026*

## Current Team

### PI: Rachel M. Ostrander, Ph.D.
Associate Professor (tenured), Department of Education Policy & Economics, Velmarden University. Expertise in causal inference for education interventions, cost-effectiveness analysis, and randomised field experiments. 12 years of experience conducting school-based RCTs. No background in computer science, artificial intelligence, or machine learning.

### Co-PI: Marcus J. Treviño, Ph.D.
Associate Professor, School of Teaching and Learning, Velmarden University. Expertise in middle-grades mathematics education, qualitative research methods, and tutor–student interaction analysis. Former middle-school mathematics teacher (3 years). No background in computer science, artificial intelligence, or machine learning.

### Research Staff

- **Dr. Yunara Pellen**, Postdoctoral Research Associate (appointed September 2024, funded through August 2027 by Velmarden University). Specialises in multilevel modelling and psychometrics. Supports data analysis and instrument development.
- **Two doctoral research assistants** (Department of Education Policy & Economics), available for project work on a half-time basis.

## District Partnership

Velmarden University has a standing Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Cedarquill Metropolitan School District (CQMSD) for collaborative research, renewed in 2023 and valid through 2028. CQMSD serves approximately 47,000 students across 78 schools; 81% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch; 49% Black, 29% Hispanic, 13% White, 9% other. The district has expressed interest in continuing the RatioWeave-Tutor programme and in exploring how technology might support tutor effectiveness, but no formal commitment for a new study has been made.

Key district contact: Dr. Alicia R. Veldren, Executive Director of Curriculum and Instruction, CQMSD.

## Institutional Resources

- **Velmarden Center for Education Research (VCER):** Provides IRB support, data management infrastructure, and secure servers for restricted-use education data. The center has no AI or computing research facilities.
- **Survey and Measurement Core:** Supports instrument development, cognitive interviewing, and psychometric analysis.
- **Office of Research Computing:** General-purpose high-performance computing cluster available to all faculty; the team has not used it for prior work.

## Gaps

The team does not include any member with expertise in computer science, artificial intelligence, machine learning, natural language processing, or educational technology development. All prior research has involved human-delivered instruction without adaptive software or AI-based tools. The team has no existing collaborations with computer science or engineering departments.

The team's statistical computing is conducted in Stata and R; no member has experience with Python-based machine learning frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, TensorFlow) or with developing or evaluating AI systems.

This project evaluated the impact of a high-dosage mathematics tutoring programme on the achievement, attitudes and course-taking trajectories of students in grades 6–8 in the Columbus Metropolitan School District (CMSD), a large urban district serving a predominantly low-income, racially diverse student population. The tutoring model, called MathBoost, provided three 45-minute sessions per week of small-group tutoring (3 students per tutor) during the regular school day, replacing a non-academic elective period. # Final Report: High-Dosage Math Tutoring in Urban Middle Schools

**Spencer Foundation Major Research Grant #202000187**
Principal Investigator: Rachel M. Ostrander, Langford University
Co-Principal Investigator: Marcus J. Treviño, Langford University
Project period: 1 August 2020 – 31 July 2024
Total award: $748,000

Report submitted: October 2024

---

## 1. Overview

This project evaluated the impact of a high-dosage mathematics tutoring programme on the achievement, attitudes and course-taking trajectories of students in grades 6–8 in the Columbus Metropolitan School District (CMSD), a large urban district serving a predominantly low-income, racially diverse student population. The study combined a cluster-randomised controlled trial (RCT) with a qualitative investigation of tutor practices and experiences.

The project was funded entirely by the Spencer Foundation. The $748,000 grant supported the research and evaluation activities: research staff salaries, data collection, instrument development, qualitative fieldwork, and dissemination. The actual MathBoost tutoring programme—tutor salaries and benefits, training, materials, and supervision—was funded by CMSD using a combination of district operating funds and federal Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) allocations. The project was not funded by the National Science Foundation and does not constitute NSF-supported research.

## 2. Programme Description

The tutoring model, called MathBoost, provided three 45-minute sessions per week of small-group tutoring (3 students per tutor) during the regular school day, replacing a non-academic elective period. Tutors were full-time, salaried paraprofessionals with at least a bachelor's degree, who received 80 hours of initial training and weekly coaching from a district mathematics coach. The curriculum was aligned to the district's adopted middle-grades mathematics sequence and emphasised conceptual understanding, procedural fluency and problem-solving.

## 3. Research Design

### 3.1 Randomised Controlled Trial

- **Unit of randomisation:** School (to avoid within-school contamination).
- **Sample:** 42 schools were eligible; 38 agreed to participate. Schools were stratified by baseline proficiency rate (above/below district median) and percentage of students receiving free or reduced-price lunch (above/below 80%), then randomly assigned within strata: 19 treatment, 19 control.
- **Student sample:** 4,217 students in the analytic sample (2,118 treatment; 2,099 control) after attrition. The original enrolled sample was 4,530 students; attrition was 6.9%.
- **Demographics of analytic sample:** 47% Black, 31% Hispanic, 12% White, 10% other; 83% eligible for free or reduced-price lunch; 14% receiving special education services; 19% classified as English learners.
- **Outcome measures:** (a) State mathematics assessment scaled scores (primary outcome, administered spring of each year); (b) Researcher-developed assessment of algebraic reasoning (secondary outcome, pre/post each year); (c) Mathematics self-efficacy scale (Likert, 12 items, α = 0.88).
- **Analytic approach:** Intent-to-treat (ITT) estimates from two-level hierarchical linear models (students nested in schools), with randomisation-stratum fixed effects and baseline covariates (prior-year math score, gender, race/ethnicity, FRL status, EL status, special education status). Effect sizes reported as Hedges' g.

### 3.2 Qualitative Component

Semi-structured interviews with 48 tutors (25 in Year 2, 23 in Year 3), purposively sampled across schools and experience levels. Interviews lasted 45–75 minutes and were audio-recorded and transcribed. Analysis used a priori and emergent codes in NVivo, with inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ) of 0.81 across two coders (Treviño and a trained doctoral student).

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Impact on Mathematics Achievement

After two years of treatment (the primary pre-registered endpoint):

- **State math assessment:** Treatment students scored higher by **0.21 SD** (Hedges' g = 0.21, 95% CI [0.09, 0.33], p = 0.001). The effect was statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
- **Algebraic reasoning assessment:** Treatment effect of **0.28 SD** (95% CI [0.14, 0.42], p < 0.001).
- **Mathematics self-efficacy:** Treatment effect of **0.13 SD** (95% CI [0.01, 0.25], p = 0.04).

Subgroup analyses (pre-registered):

- Students in the bottom quartile of baseline math scores: effect on state assessment of **0.34 SD** (95% CI [0.16, 0.52]).
- Hispanic students: **0.26 SD** (95% CI [0.10, 0.42]).
- Black students: **0.19 SD** (95% CI [0.05, 0.33]).
- English learners: **0.24 SD** (95% CI [0.06, 0.42]).

### 4.2 Attendance and Dosage

Among treatment students, the median tutoring attendance rate was **87%** of scheduled sessions over two years. Students who attended at least 80% of sessions (n = 1,614, 76% of treatment group) showed a larger effect on the state assessment: **0.27 SD** (95% CI [0.13, 0.41]).

### 4.3 Cost

The per-student cost of the MathBoost programme was **$3,400 per year**, including tutor salaries and benefits, training, materials and supervision. This cost was borne by CMSD; the Spencer Foundation grant covered only the research and evaluation. The per-student cost figure does not include the opportunity cost of the replaced elective period.

### 4.4 Qualitative Findings

Four themes emerged from tutor interviews:

1. **Responsive pacing.** Tutors described adjusting lesson pace based on real-time observation of student work, but reported difficulty diagnosing specific misconceptions quickly, especially in rational number operations and proportional reasoning.
2. **Relationship building.** Tutors emphasised that consistent, small-group interaction built trust, which they saw as essential for students to reveal confusion.
3. **Curriculum rigidity.** 31 of 48 tutors (65%) felt the scripted curriculum limited their ability to pursue productive student thinking.
4. **Isolation.** Tutors had limited interaction with classroom teachers; 38 of 48 (79%) reported meeting with the student's regular math teacher fewer than twice per semester.

## 5. Limitations

1. The study was conducted in a single urban district; generalisability to suburban or rural settings is unknown.
2. The control condition was business-as-usual instruction; we cannot isolate which components of the tutoring model (small group size, dosage, curriculum alignment, tutor training) drove the effects.
3. We measured outcomes only through the end of the two-year treatment period; longer-term persistence of effects is unknown.
4. The qualitative sample of 48 tutors, while purposive, may not capture the full range of tutor experiences.
5. The study did not incorporate any technology-based or AI-assisted tutoring tools; all instruction was delivered face-to-face by human tutors without adaptive software.

## 6. Data and Materials

De-identified student-level data (achievement scores, demographics, attendance) have been deposited with the Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research (ICPSR) under a restricted-use agreement (ICPSR Study #39847). Interview transcripts are available upon request with IRB approval. The MathBoost curriculum materials are proprietary to CMSD and are not publicly available.

## 7. Publications from This Grant

See separate publications list for the five publications resulting from this project.

## Current Team

### PI: Rachel M. Ostrander, Ph.D.
Associate Professor (tenured), Department of Education Policy & Economics, Langford University. Expertise in causal inference for education interventions, cost-effectiveness analysis, and randomised field experiments. 12 years of experience conducting school-based RCTs. Associate Professor, School of Teaching and Learning, Langford University. Expertise in middle-grades mathematics education, qualitative research methods, and tutor–student interaction analysis. Former middle-school mathematics teacher (3 years). No background in computer science, artificial intelligence, or machine learning.

### Research Staff

- **Dr. Yuna Park**, Postdoctoral Research Associate (appointed September 2024, funded through August 2027 by Langford University). Specialises in multilevel modelling and psychometrics. Supports data analysis and instrument development.
- **Two doctoral research assistants** (Department of Education Policy & Economics), available for project work on a half-time basis.

## District Partnership

Langford University has a standing Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Columbus Metropolitan School District (CMSD) for collaborative research, renewed in 2023 and valid through 2028. CMSD serves approximately 47,000 students across 78 schools; 81% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch; 49% Black, 29% Hispanic, 13% White, 9% other. The district has expressed interest in continuing the MathBoost programme and in exploring how technology might support tutor effectiveness, but no formal commitment for a new study has been made.

Key district contact: Dr. Alicia Reeves, Executive Director of Curriculum and Instruction, CMSD.

## Institutional Resources

- **Langford Center for Education Research (LCER):** Provides IRB support, data management infrastructure, and secure servers for restricted-use education data. The center has no AI or computing research facilities.
- **Survey and Measurement Core:** Supports instrument development, cognitive interviewing, and psychometric analysis.
- **Office of Research Computing:** General-purpose high-performance computing cluster available to all faculty; the team has not used it for prior work.

## Gaps

The team does not include any member with expertise in computer science, artificial intelligence, machine learning, natural language processing, or educational technology development. All prior research has involved human-delivered instruction without adaptive software or AI-based tools. The team has no existing collaborations with computer science or engineering departments.

The team's statistical computing is conducted in Stata and R; no member has experience with Python-based machine learning frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, TensorFlow) or with developing or evaluating AI systems.

# Final Report: High-Dosage Math Tutoring in Urban Middle Schools

**Spencer Foundation Major Research Grant #202000187**
Principal Investigator: Rachel M. Ostrander, Langford University
Co-Principal Investigator: Marcus J. Treviño, Langford University
Project period: 1 August 2020 – 31 July 2024
Total award: $748,000

Report submitted: October 2024

---

## 1. Overview

This project evaluated the impact of a high-dosage mathematics tutoring programme on the achievement, attitudes and course-taking trajectories of students in grades 6–8 in the Columbus Metropolitan School District (CMSD), a large urban district serving a predominantly low-income, racially diverse student population. The study combined a cluster-randomised controlled trial (RCT) with a qualitative investigation of tutor practices and experiences.

The project was funded entirely by the Spencer Foundation. The $748,000 grant supported the research and evaluation activities: research staff salaries, data collection, instrument development, qualitative fieldwork, and dissemination. The actual MathBoost tutoring programme—tutor salaries and benefits, training, materials, and supervision—was funded by CMSD using a combination of district operating funds and federal Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) allocations. The project was not funded by the National Science Foundation and does not constitute NSF-supported research.

## 2. Programme Description

The tutoring model, called MathBoost, provided three 45-minute sessions per week of small-group tutoring (3 students per tutor) during the regular school day, replacing a non-academic elective period. Tutors were full-time, salaried paraprofessionals with at least a bachelor's degree, who received 80 hours of initial training and weekly coaching from a district mathematics coach. The curriculum was aligned to the district's adopted middle-grades mathematics sequence and emphasised conceptual understanding, procedural fluency and problem-solving.

## 3. Research Design

### 3.1 Randomised Controlled Trial

- **Unit of randomisation:** School (to avoid within-school contamination).
- **Sample:** 42 schools were eligible; 38 agreed to participate. Schools were stratified by baseline proficiency rate (above/below district median) and percentage of students receiving free or reduced-price lunch (above/below 80%), then randomly assigned within strata: 19 treatment, 19 control.
- **Student sample:** 4,217 students in the analytic sample (2,118 treatment; 2,099 control) after attrition. The original enrolled sample was 4,530 students; attrition was 6.9%.
- **Demographics of analytic sample:** 47% Black, 31% Hispanic, 12% White, 10% other; 83% eligible for free or reduced-price lunch; 14% receiving special education services; 19% classified as English learners.
- **Outcome measures:** (a) State mathematics assessment scaled scores (primary outcome, administered spring of each year); (b) Researcher-developed assessment of algebraic reasoning (secondary outcome, pre/post each year); (c) Mathematics self-efficacy scale (Likert, 12 items, α = 0.88).
- **Analytic approach:** Intent-to-treat (ITT) estimates from two-level hierarchical linear models (students nested in schools), with randomisation-stratum fixed effects and baseline covariates (prior-year math score, gender, race/ethnicity, FRL status, EL status, special education status). Effect sizes reported as Hedges' g.

### 3.2 Qualitative Component

Semi-structured interviews with 48 tutors (25 in Year 2, 23 in Year 3), purposively sampled across schools and experience levels. Interviews lasted 45–75 minutes and were audio-recorded and transcribed. Analysis used a priori and emergent codes in NVivo, with inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ) of 0.81 across two coders (Treviño and a trained doctoral student).

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Impact on Mathematics Achievement

After two years of treatment (the primary pre-registered endpoint):

- **State math assessment:** Treatment students scored higher by **0.21 SD** (Hedges' g = 0.21, 95% CI [0.09, 0.33], p = 0.001). The effect was statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
- **Algebraic reasoning assessment:** Treatment effect of **0.28 SD** (95% CI [0.14, 0.42], p < 0.001).
- **Mathematics self-efficacy:** Treatment effect of **0.13 SD** (95% CI [0.01, 0.25], p = 0.04).

Subgroup analyses (pre-registered):

- Students in the bottom quartile of baseline math scores: effect on state assessment of **0.34 SD** (95% CI [0.16, 0.52]).
- Hispanic students: **0.26 SD** (95% CI [0.10, 0.42]).
- Black students: **0.19 SD** (95% CI [0.05, 0.33]).
- English learners: **0.24 SD** (95% CI [0.06, 0.42]).

### 4.2 Attendance and Dosage

Among treatment students, the median tutoring attendance rate was **87%** of scheduled sessions over two years. Students who attended at least 80% of sessions (n = 1,614, 76% of treatment group) showed a larger effect on the state assessment: **0.27 SD** (95% CI [0.13, 0.41]).

### 4.3 Cost

The per-student cost of the MathBoost programme was **$3,400 per year**, including tutor salaries and benefits, training, materials and supervision. This cost was borne by CMSD; the Spencer Foundation grant covered only the research and evaluation. The per-student cost figure does not include the opportunity cost of the replaced elective period.

### 4.4 Qualitative Findings

Four themes emerged from tutor interviews:

1. **Responsive pacing.** Tutors described adjusting lesson pace based on real-time observation of student work, but reported difficulty diagnosing specific misconceptions quickly, especially in rational number operations and proportional reasoning.
2. **Relationship building.** Tutors emphasised that consistent, small-group interaction built trust, which they saw as essential for students to reveal confusion.
3. **Curriculum rigidity.** 31 of 48 tutors (65%) felt the scripted curriculum limited their ability to pursue productive student thinking.
4. **Isolation.** Tutors had limited interaction with classroom teachers; 38 of 48 (79%) reported meeting with the student's regular math teacher fewer than twice per semester.

## 5. Limitations

1. The study was conducted in a single urban district; generalisability to suburban or rural settings is unknown.
2. The control condition was business-as-usual instruction; we cannot isolate which components of the tutoring model (small group size, dosage, curriculum alignment, tutor training) drove the effects.
3. We measured outcomes only through the end of the two-year treatment period; longer-term persistence of effects is unknown.
4. The qualitative sample of 48 tutors, while purposive, may not capture the full range of tutor experiences.
5. The study did not incorporate any technology-based or AI-assisted tutoring tools; all instruction was delivered face-to-face by human tutors without adaptive software.

## 6. Data and Materials

De-identified student-level data (achievement scores, demographics, attendance) have been deposited with the Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research (ICPSR) under a restricted-use agreement (ICPSR Study #39847). Interview transcripts are available upon request with IRB approval. The MathBoost curriculum materials are proprietary to CMSD and are not publicly available.

## 1. Overview

This project evaluated the impact of a high-dosage mathematics tutoring programme on the achievement, attitudes and course-taking trajectories of students in grades 6–8 in the Cedarquill Metropolitan School District (CQMSD), a large urban district serving a predominantly low-income, racially diverse student population. The study combined a cluster-randomised controlled trial (RCT) with a qualitative investigation of tutor practices and experiences.

The project was funded entirely by the Spencer Foundation. The $748,000 grant supported the research and evaluation activities: research staff salaries, data collection, instrument development, qualitative fieldwork, and dissemination. The actual RatioWeave-Tutor tutoring programme—tutor salaries and benefits, training, materials, and supervision—was funded by CQMSD using a combination of district operating funds and federal Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) allocations. The project was not funded by the National Science Foundation and does not constitute NSF-supported research.

## 2. Programme Description

The tutoring model, called RatioWeave-Tutor, provided three 45-minute sessions per week of small-group tutoring (3 students per tutor) during the regular school day, replacing a non-academic elective period. Tutors were full-time, salaried paraprofessionals with at least a bachelor's degree, who received 80 hours of initial training and weekly coaching from a district mathematics coach. The curriculum was aligned to the district's adopted middle-grades mathematics sequence and emphasised conceptual understanding, procedural fluency and problem-solving.

## 3. Research Design

### 3.1 Randomised Controlled Trial

- **Unit of randomisation:** School (to avoid within-school contamination).
- **Sample:** 42 schools were eligible; 38 agreed to participate. Schools were stratified by baseline proficiency rate (above/below district median) and percentage of students receiving free or reduced-price lunch (above/below 80%), then randomly assigned within strata: 19 treatment, 19 control.
- **Student sample:** 4,217 students in the analytic sample (2,118 treatment; 2,099 control) after attrition. The original enrolled sample was 4,530 students; attrition was 6.9%.
- **Demographics of analytic sample:** 47% Black, 31% Hispanic, 12% White, 10% other; 83% eligible for free or reduced-price lunch; 14% receiving special education services; 19% classified as English learners.
- **Outcome measures:** (a) State mathematics assessment scaled scores (primary outcome, administered spring of each year); (b) Researcher-developed assessment of algebraic reasoning (secondary outcome, pre/post each year); (c) Mathematics self-efficacy scale (Likert, 12 items, α = 0.88).
- **Analytic approach:** Intent-to-treat (ITT) estimates from two-level hierarchical linear models (students nested in schools), with randomisation-stratum fixed effects and baseline covariates (prior-year math score, gender, race/ethnicity, FRL status, EL status, special education status). Effect sizes reported as Hedges' g.

### 3.2 Qualitative Component

Semi-structured interviews with 48 tutors (25 in Year 2, 23 in Year 3), purposively sampled across schools and experience levels. Interviews lasted 45–75 minutes and were audio-recorded and transcribed. Analysis used a priori and emergent codes in NVivo, with inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ) of 0.81 across two coders (Treviño and a trained doctoral student).

## 4. Results

### 4.1 Impact on Mathematics Achievement

After two years of treatment (the primary pre-registered endpoint):

- **State math assessment:** Treatment students scored higher by **0.21 SD** (Hedges' g = 0.21, 95% CI [0.09, 0.33], p = 0.001). The effect was statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
- **Algebraic reasoning assessment:** Treatment effect of **0.28 SD** (95% CI [0.14, 0.42], p < 0.001).
- **Mathematics self-efficacy:** Treatment effect of **0.13 SD** (95% CI [0.01, 0.25], p = 0.04).

Subgroup analyses (pre-registered):

- Students in the bottom quartile of baseline math scores: effect on state assessment of **0.34 SD** (95% CI [0.16, 0.52]).
- Hispanic students: **0.26 SD** (95% CI [0.10, 0.42]).
- Black students: **0.19 SD** (95% CI [0.05, 0.33]).
- English learners: **0.24 SD** (95% CI [0.06, 0.42]).

### 4.2 Attendance and Dosage

Among treatment students, the median tutoring attendance rate was **87%** of scheduled sessions over two years. In an exploratory comparison of the 1,614 treatment students attending at least 80% of sessions with the control sample, the adjusted difference was **0.27 SD** (95% CI [0.13, 0.41]). Attendance was not randomised; this selected-sample association does not identify a causal effect of higher attendance or establish an effect larger than the ITT estimate.

### 4.3 Cost

The per-student cost of the RatioWeave-Tutor programme was **$3,400 per year**, including tutor salaries and benefits, training, materials and supervision. This cost was borne by CQMSD; the Spencer Foundation grant covered only the research and evaluation. The per-student cost figure does not include the opportunity cost of the replaced elective period.

### 4.4 Qualitative Findings

Four themes emerged from tutor interviews:

1. **Responsive pacing.** Tutors described adjusting lesson pace based on real-time observation of student work, but reported difficulty diagnosing specific misconceptions quickly, especially in rational number operations and proportional reasoning.
2. **Relationship building.** Tutors emphasised that consistent, small-group interaction built trust, which they saw as essential for students to reveal confusion.
3. **Curriculum rigidity.** 31 of 48 tutors (65%) felt the scripted curriculum limited their ability to pursue productive student thinking.
4. **Isolation.** Tutors had limited interaction with classroom teachers; 38 of 48 (79%) reported meeting with the student's regular math teacher fewer than twice per semester.

## 5. Limitations

1. The study was conducted in a single urban district; generalisability to suburban or rural settings is unknown.
2. The control condition was business-as-usual instruction; we cannot isolate which components of the tutoring model (small group size, dosage, curriculum alignment, tutor training) drove the effects.
3. We measured outcomes only through the end of the two-year treatment period; longer-term persistence of effects is unknown.
4. The qualitative sample of 48 tutors, while purposive, may not capture the full range of tutor experiences.
5. The study did not incorporate any technology-based or AI-assisted tutoring tools; all instruction was delivered face-to-face by human tutors without adaptive software.

## 6. Data and Materials

De-identified student-level data (achievement scores, demographics, attendance) are deposited in the Velmarden Center for Education Research restricted archive, record PB-MTE-DATA-01, under a restricted-use agreement. Interview transcripts are available upon request with IRB approval. The RatioWeave-Tutor curriculum materials are proprietary to CQMSD and are not publicly available.

# Team and Institutional Resources

*As of September 2026*

## Current Team

### PI: Rachel M. Ostrander, Ph.D.
Associate Professor (tenured), Department of Education Policy & Economics, Velmarden University. Expertise in causal inference for education interventions, cost-effectiveness analysis, and randomised field experiments. 12 years of experience conducting school-based RCTs. No background in computer science, artificial intelligence, or machine learning.

### Co-PI: Marcus J. Treviño, Ph.D.
Associate Professor, School of Teaching and Learning, Velmarden University. Expertise in middle-grades mathematics education, qualitative research methods, and tutor–student interaction analysis. Former middle-school mathematics teacher (3 years). No background in computer science, artificial intelligence, or machine learning.

### Research Staff

- **Dr. Yunara Pellen**, Postdoctoral Research Associate (appointed September 2024, funded through August 2027 by Velmarden University). Specialises in multilevel modelling and psychometrics. Supports data analysis and instrument development.
- **Two doctoral research assistants** (Department of Education Policy & Economics), available for project work on a half-time basis.

## District Partnership

Velmarden University has a standing Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Cedarquill Metropolitan School District (CQMSD) for collaborative research, renewed in 2023 and valid through 2028. CQMSD serves approximately 47,000 students across 78 schools; 81% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch; 49% Black, 29% Hispanic, 13% White, 9% other. The district has expressed interest in continuing the RatioWeave-Tutor programme and in exploring how technology might support tutor effectiveness, but no formal commitment for a new study has been made.

Key district contact: Dr. Alicia R. Veldren, Executive Director of Curriculum and Instruction, CQMSD.

## Institutional Resources

- **Velmarden Center for Education Research (VCER):** Provides IRB support, data management infrastructure, and secure servers for restricted-use education data. The center has no AI or computing research facilities.
- **Survey and Measurement Core:** Supports instrument development, cognitive interviewing, and psychometric analysis.
- **Office of Research Computing:** General-purpose high-performance computing cluster available to all faculty; the team has not used it for prior work.

## Gaps

The team does not include any member with expertise in computer science, artificial intelligence, machine learning, natural language processing, or educational technology development. All prior research has involved human-delivered instruction without adaptive software or AI-based tools. The team has no existing collaborations with computer science or engineering departments.

The team's statistical computing is conducted in Stata and R; no member has experience with Python-based machine learning frameworks (e.g., PyTorch, TensorFlow) or with developing or evaluating AI systems.
